lesson.title: The Signal You Didn't Send: Understanding Noise
lesson.summary: Noise is the collection of random, unwanted electrical disturbances present on every real channel, and the signal to noise ratio, the comparison between wanted signal power and this background disturbance, determines whether a receiver can actually recover what was sent.
lesson.body:
Every real communication channel carries more than the signal a transmitter intentionally puts on it. Random, unwanted electrical or electromagnetic disturbances are always present too, and collectively these disturbances are called noise. Unlike attenuation, which reduces the signal you sent, noise adds something you never sent in the first place, and a receiver has to somehow separate the two before it can recover the original bits.

Noise comes from several distinct physical sources. Thermal noise, sometimes called Johnson-Nyquist noise, is caused by the random motion of electrons inside any conductor at a temperature above absolute zero, and it is present in every wire, antenna, and amplifier regardless of what traffic is on the line, setting a hard floor below which no signal can be reliably detected. Crosstalk is a related but different problem in cables: signal energy leaking from one wire pair into a neighboring pair, for instance between adjacent twisted pairs inside the same Ethernet cable. Impulse noise is sudden, short bursts of high energy from sources like lightning, motors switching on, or faulty electrical connections, and it can corrupt a short stretch of a transmission even when the average noise level is otherwise low.

The relationship that determines whether a receiver can actually recover the signal is the signal to noise ratio, or SNR, which compares the power of the wanted signal to the power of the noise it is competing with. SNR is usually expressed in decibels: SNR in dB equals 10 times log base 10 of signal power divided by noise power. Suppose a receiver measures a signal at 1 milliwatt, 0 dBm, and a noise floor of 0.01 milliwatt, negative 20 dBm, on the same channel. The SNR is 0 minus negative 20, or 20 dB, meaning the signal is 100 times more powerful than the noise, a comfortable margin for reliable reception. Wi-Fi engineers commonly treat an SNR above roughly 25 dB as excellent and below roughly 10 dB as marginal, since a low SNR forces devices to fall back to slower, more robust modulation schemes or start losing frames outright.

Notice how this connects directly to the idea of a signal itself: a signal only carries information because a receiver can distinguish its different states, different voltage levels, phases, or amplitudes, from one another. Noise makes that distinction harder by blurring the boundaries between those states, and if the noise power ever becomes comparable to the signal power, the receiver simply cannot tell which state was sent. This is also why attenuation and noise form such a dangerous combination on any real link: attenuation shrinks the signal over distance while the noise floor stays roughly constant, so every additional bit of attenuation directly eats into the SNR margin the receiver depends on to do its job.
